title: The Wedding Where I Finally Learned to Listen
script: Narrator: [warmly] Last month, I went to my cousin's wedding, and something happened there that I still think about often.
Narrator: During the dinner, I was sitting next to my great-uncle, a man who talks slowly and tells very long stories.
Narrator: [impatient] In the past, I usually found an excuse to leave when he started talking, because his stories felt endless and repetitive to me.
Narrator: This time, my phone battery had died, so I could not escape into my phone like I normally would have.
Narrator: [gently] He began telling a story about how he and my great-aunt built their small family shop sixty years ago.
Narrator: [slowly interested] At first, I listened only because I had no other choice, but slowly, the story began to pull me in completely.
Narrator: He described their first difficult year, the long working days, and how relatives helped them keep the shop open.
Narrator: [surprised] I realized I had never actually asked him about his life before, even though he had been part of our family my whole life.
Narrator: [softly] When he finished, he looked at me and said, thank you for listening, nobody has time for old stories anymore.
Narrator: [touched] That sentence hit me hard, because it was true. I had never given him my full attention before that night.
Narrator: I understood then that listening is a form of adab too, maybe one of the quietest and most overlooked forms there is.
Narrator: [determined] Since that wedding, I try to sit with older relatives more often, and I leave my phone in my pocket when they speak.
Narrator: It is a small change, but full attention can communicate respect in a way an expensive gift may not.
Narrator: [grateful] My great-uncle passed away a few weeks after that wedding, so I am grateful I finally listened, while there was still time.

The uncle died soon after the conversation

quiz.explanation: Patient listening revealed that the earlier judgment was unfair.
